author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: State surveillance adds to teachers’ multiple burden
content:
CAGAYAN DE ORO — A public school head expressed her strong denunciation as she narrated the recent series of surveillance by alleged state agents to some teachers in Pitogo, Zamboanga del Sur.

“If they won’t stop red-tagging, profiling, tailing, harassing, and intimidating us, we will file a case,” Liza Idiang, chairperson of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) Zamboanga Peninsula Region, told Bulatlat in an interview.

Idiang, a public school head at Balongbalong Elementary School in Pitogo town, said the surveillance started on July 25, when two individuals who introduced themselves as personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) went to her residence, asking for her whereabouts.

Since she was in Pagadian City that time, the alleged police personnel proceeded to the residence of another teacher, asking if they were planning to stage a protest action for the State of the Nation Address (SONA) of Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and if the latter was recruited by Idiang to join ACT.

The residence of another ACT Zamboanga Peninsula member in Pitogo, Idiang said, was also allegedly visited by state agents.

Another person who also introduced himself as police personnel visited Idiang’s house on July 26. This time, she was able to confront the person. The latter allegedly uttered red-tagging remarks against their organization.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Revilla granted bail as elderly political prisoners remain in jail
content:
If the courts can extend humanitarian consideration to a politician accused of multimillion-peso plunder—who has yet to comply with the order to return P124.5 million to the Philippine Treasury in an earlier PDAF scam—why is the same compassion denied to innocent, elderly, and gravely ill political prisoners?

MANILA — Human rights groups Kapatid, the Laya Campaign to Free All Political Prisoners, and the Samahan ng Ex-Detainees Laban sa Detensyon at Aresto (Selda) on August 3 criticized the Sandiganbayan’s grant of bail to former senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr.,

They said that the ruling exposes a “double standard” in the country’s justice system as elderly and ailing political prisoners remain behind bars despite years of pretrial detention.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division granted Revilla provisional liberty on July 31 after he posted a P1-million cash bond in connection with his malversation case involving an alleged P92.8-million ghost flood control project in Bulacan.

Laya and Selda described the ruling as an “injustice.”

“A justice system that favors grafters and plunderers over those who fight for accountability is one that runs on impunity and dispenses injustice,” the groups said.

They repeated their call to “Jail the corrupt and free all political prisoners.”

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Media group slams VP’s criticism of Philippine journalism
content:
It is atrocious for the second-highest official of the land to make such generalizations on journalists and media workers who remain committed to reporting on the truth despite continuing attacks.

CAGAYAN DE ORO — A group of journalists denounced the remarks of Vice President Sara Duterte who criticized the state of Philippine journalism falling short of international standards.

In a statement, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) acknowledged the reality that newsrooms are not safe from mistakes. But it said that it is atrocious for the second-highest official of the land to make such generalizations on journalists and media workers who remain committed to reporting on the truth despite continuing attacks.

“By denigrating Philippine media, [Duterte] is unleashing one of the tactics straight out of a dictator’s playbook: controlling information by demonizing the independent press and weaponizing social media for her propaganda,” NUJP said.

Duterte, who has been a subject of an ongoing impeachment trial, issued the remarks after she was asked about the apparent “practice” of the dominant media to put her family in a bad light. In her comments, she differentiated the ways of local and international media when it comes to presenting their reports. She also accused the media of “worshipping money.”

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Cumpio, Domequil appeal financing terrorism conviction to higher court
content:
Terrorism laws like the Anti-Terrorism Law and Terrorism Financing along with the insidious use of military assets to fabricate narratives are weaponized to persecute the likes of Frenchie and Marielle.

CEBU CITY—The legal team of community journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio and church worker Marielle Domequil filed an appeal before the Court of Appeals here on August 3 to overturn the guilty verdict on terrorism financing.

“We’ve submitted a joint appellants’ brief to the Court of Appeals where we delineated the reasons why we believe that the Regional Trial Court in Tacloban wrongly convicted both Frenchie and Marielle,” said Atty. Julianne Agpalo, legal counsel of Cumpio and Domequil.

Agpalo explained that “after the submission of the appeal, the state through the Office of the Solicitor General will be given time to respond to the appellant’s brief we submitted to which we will also respond to. From there, the Court of Appeals will review all documents submitted, then it will decide whether to affirm or, hopefully, reverse the judgment of the RTC in Tacloban”

As convenors of Stand with Samar-Leyte, a network of progressive groups in Eastern Visayas, Agpalo said that Cumpio and Domequil’s works tied to the said network are “lawful and humanitarian and only aimed to alleviate the burdens of the people in the region.”

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Drought spells hunger for farmers
content:
ISABELA – Parched lands. Crops are dying while some grow unevenly. Worms and pests swarming.  Such are the farmlands beside the Cagayan river, and farmers worry about what little they could harvest.

“It’s frustrating to see the crops here,” said farmer Pablo Canseran in the vernacular, showing the damages of his crops. He is cultivating one hectare of corn this season, but his estimated loss has already reached 80 sacks of corn, significantly higher than what he could save: only 14 sacks. “We are losing more, barely enough to cover our debts,” he lamented.

Drought is not a new problem. However, the irrigation system remains insufficient. Farmers are forced to rent a water tractor machine for P300/day ($6), and additional P500 ($10) for gasoline expenses, just to get water from the river. But even that wouldn’t suffice, especially in this season of drought.

“The crops did not grow properly because there was no rain. The heat was so intense that they got infested with worms,” said farmer-leader Doringa Aberion in the vernacular. “Other crops grow but without fruits.”

In March 2026, the provincial government of Isabela declared that the entire province under a state of calamity through a Sangguniang Panlalawigan resolution, due to prolonged dry spell. author: Aaron Ernest Cruz
title: Indigenous community rising up against mining in Nueva Vizcaya
content:
MANILA –  Zesirie Enggo, 26, from Bugkalot tribe and convenor of Kasibu Inter-Tribal Response towards Ecological Development (KIRED) is in the frontline of struggle against the North Luzon Mineral Resource Center (NLMRC) operations in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya .

In an interview with Bulatlat , Enggo talked about the impacts of mining on the environment and their community. “When I was a child, the river was wide, but now it has become just a channel of water that came from the mine,” Enggo said.

For Enggo, life was peaceful back then. The family’s livelihood is farming, which she said, supported her and her siblings’ needs. She is the second child in a brood of four.

She earned a degree in criminology from a private university. However, job opportunities are rare so she decided to go back to farming.  “I’ve tried looking for a job many times but still haven’t found one. I have become more knowledgeable and have seen the value of farming, so this has become my livelihood,” she told Bulatlat in an interview.

This is why when they discovered that an exploration permit was granted by the Mines and Geoscience Bureau (MGB) to NLMRC, they stood against it.

Last July 10, Enggo, along with other delegates from Nueva Vizcaya, went to Manila to tell their story at the State of the Philippine Environment organized by various groups.

author: Danilo Arao
title: Iyak
content:
Huwag hayaan ang “crocodile tears” ng mga nasa kapangyarihan.

Dahil napaluha siya, makabagbag-damdamin para sa unang ginang ang ikalimang State of the Nation Address (SONA) ng pangulo noong Hulyo 27. Kung sabagay, nakakaiyak naman talaga dahil marami siyang hindi sinabi.

Kumusta ang panawagang taasan ang sahod ng mga manggagawa? Ano ang tindig ng pangulo tungkol sa tunay na repormang agraryo para sa mga magsasaka, pati na sa pagkilala sa lupang ninuno ng mga katutubo?

Kahit na may mga binanggit siya tungkol sa ilang planong pababain ang buwis at singil sa kuryente, hindi ba’t mas mainam na sagutin muna ang matagal nang panawagan ng iba’t ibang sektor ng lipunan? Aanhin ang kakarampot na ginhawa kung hindi pa rin komportable ang pangkabuuang kalagayan?

Bukod sa pera, nariyan din ang problema ng kawalang katiyakan kaya nananatiling pangarap ang magandang buhay para sa mga nasa laylayan ng lipunan.

Sa kabila ng retorika ng pagpapataas ng posibleng mautang mula sa gobyerno para magkaroon ng sariling bahay, mistulang “bahala na kayong magbayad” ang mensahe ng pangulo sa panahong talamak ang kontraktuwalisasyon kaya hindi sigurado kung may trabaho pa makalipas ang ilang buwan. At kahit na permanente naman sa trabaho, babalik pa rin sa isa pang pundamental na problema ng mababang sahod.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Power beneath the surface: Mining, politics and the Marcos dev’t agenda
content:
Indigenous Peoples, and environmental groups protested in front of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) and the Department of Environment and National Resources (DENR) after the recent mining exploration activities of North Luzon Mineral Resource Corporation (NLMRC) in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya.

“We hope there will be no more mining projects and that these mining companies will leave, because I know that mining is not the only way a community can achieve progress.”

MANILA — For Indigenous peoples in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya, there is no justice in Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s ‘just’ energy transition.

Growing up in the fertile rice fields of the province, Bugkalot-Ilongot resident Zesirie Enggo chose to till the same land that had sustained generations of their community.

On sunny days before, she recalled, a single hectare of their rice field could yield up to 100 sacks of palay.

Yet, as several mining corporations — FCF Minerals Corporation, Oceana Gold Philippines Inc. and now North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC) — take interest in the richness of their mountains and soil, their lives, livelihood and means of subsistence absorb the blow.

“Marcos is at the top, and those at the lower levels cannot be the only ones held accountable.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — Since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s “ mahiya naman kayo ” remarks at his State of the National Address (SONA) last year, who has been held accountable so far over the multibillion-peso flood control scam, the country’s so-called largest corruption scandal?

Among those detained so far are several officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), private contractors Curlee and Sarah Discaya, former senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, and incumbent senator Jinggoy Estrada.

title: Canada-Philippines ‘strategic partnership’ for whom?
content:
Hundreds protest during Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s visit in Vancouver Canada (Photo by BAYAN BC)

“Security, development, and economic growth for whom? For whom is this going to serve? It always goes to big business, to bureaucrats, to corrupt government officials, to the same people it always goes to. And we have to expose this, because this is not economic growth, security and development of the people. This is further putting the people in precarious, dangerous, exploitative conditions in both Canada and the Philippines.”

TORONTO – During last year’s State of the Nation Address (SONA), Ferdinand Marcos Jr. did not mention the unequal trade and military agreements with the United States. For this year’s SONA, as he ties up with another foreign power, progressives anticipate that Marcos Jr. will frame the agreements as yet another “achievement” of his administration.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Melinda Quintos de Jesus as Gawad Plaridel 2026 awardee: ‘A moment of affirmation’
content:
Melinda Quintos de Jesus speaks during the Jaime V. Ongpin Journalism Seminar in 2025. Photo courtesy of the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR).

“It’s a confirmation of worthiness, perhaps of what we are doing.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — For veteran journalist and media development advocate Melinda Quintos de Jesus, her recognition as Gawad Plaridel 2026 awardee is “a moment of affirmation.”

De Jesus, who founded the media watchdog Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) in 1989, considered the award as a significant assessment of her advocacy in defending press freedom and ensuring media accountability, as well as molding future fully equipped journalists.

“It’s a confirmation of worthiness, perhaps of what we are doing,” she told Bulatlat , dedicating the recognition as well to her colleagues in CMFR. “It drives me even more, even at my advanced age, to continue as much of the energy is still there.”

On July 20, The University of the Philippines (UP) College of Media and Communication (CMC) made the announcement for this year’s Gawad Plaridel, the highest recognition in the UP system for outstanding practitioners from different forms of media.

author: Bulatlat Staff
title: Getting the solution right
content:
A statement of Philippine media organizations and journalists on the pending anti-disinformation bills




The pending anti-disinformation bills confuse the symptoms with the disease. Instead of addressing the political, economic, and technological systems that manufacture and profit from coordinated information manipulation, they place the burden on individual expression and expand government authority over speech. This threatens democratic freedoms while leaving the real drivers of disinformation largely untouched.




As institutions and individuals whose work depends on verifying facts, exposing falsehoods, and informing the public, we have every reason to support effective measures against disinformation. Journalists are among those who experience firsthand the damage that disinformation inflicts on democratic discourse and public trust. We therefore recognize the urgency of confronting this grave challenge.




We support decisive and effective action against disinformation.




However, we believe the pending anti-disinformation bills (HB 9465 and its equivalent in the Senate) are the wrong response to a real problem.




Rather than moving to dismantle the architecture of disinformation, these measures primarily criminalize expression, expand the State’s authority to regulate speech, and create legal mechanisms that are vulnerable to misuse against journalists, critics,

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Cuba: The target of a 67-year crusade
content:
Flag of Cuba (Image from Pixabay)

How a 99-page State Department report reveals the empire’s unending war against a small island’s sovereignty

On July 20, 2026, four days after Marco Rubio convened his “Far Left Terrorism” conference in Washington, the State Department released a 99-page report titled, “ Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism .” For a report that claims to be analysis, it spends 99 pages doing nothing but justifying a blockade, the sanctions, and 67 years of war against a small island. No document better reveals the ideological character of this crusade.

Rubio has built a career on hating Cuba—an island his parents left in 1956, three years before the Revolution. They were not exiles. They were working-class immigrants who built a life in the United States. Rubio invented the exile story anyway, for cheap political gain—a social climber’s success story, now architect of U.S. imperialist counterinsurgency. As Secretary of State, he spearheaded the designation of Cuba as a State Sponsor of Terrorism. The report mirrors the man: it presents itself as rigorous research, but it is counterinsurgency—terror by another name. Rubio and the report are the same impulse dressed in different clothes: delegitimize the Cuban Revolution, criminalize its solidarity with the oppressed, and justify the siege.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Behind bars, political prisoners assert freedom
content:
Symbolic paper cranes were attached in a steel frame, holding the calls for the freedom of all political prisoners. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

MANILA – Behind bars, political prisoners found a way to document their lives, struggles, and aspirations.

This book entitled, “Pansamantalang Mundo” (Temporary World) was launched on Saturday, July 18, alongside the launch of LAYA, a national and international campaign calling for the immediate release of political prisoners in the Philippines.

“Recorded in this book is the free thought, feeling, and creativity of political prisoners whom the state has tried to silence,” said Chingbee Cruz of Paper Trail Projects, the publisher of the book, in Filipino. “This book is a firm refusal to the state’s deliberate erasure of a reasoned action in pursuit of a just society.”

The book is a product of almost two years of jail visits and writing workshops at the Correctional Institute for Women (CIW), compiling all of their works. The learning has been reciprocal: the publishers also learned about the conditions not only of political prisoners but of other persons deprived of liberty (PDL) inside the facility.
